newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua bets future on free-trade zone.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua bets future on free-trade zone.

text.p: Few goods in the world's markets carry the "Made in Nicaragua" label, but Nicaragua's new right-wing government hopes to change this by expanding its small-but-growing assembly plant zone.

In the process, Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman, who took power on Jan. 10, plans to create jobs for his impoverished nation, Latin America's second-poorest country with 52 percent of its workers unemployed or underemployed.
Aleman late on Thursday told reporters Nicaragua's new approach would be "produce to export" and he would boost exports by "promoting the maquiladora (assembly plant) zones."

In Nicaragua's maquiladora zone, called the "zona franca" here, raw materials and partially assembled parts are imported, assembled and exported largely duty free. Nearly all the assembly plants are for clothes and textiles.
The government's goal is to raise the number of workers in the maquiladora zone to 50,000 from 10,000 over the next two years, economy minister Francisco Lainez told Reuters.
Plans include improving the zones's infrastructure, energy supply and customs facilities and providing tax incentives and investment-friendly labour laws, Lainez said.

"Nicaragua's maquiladora zone is competitive but underdeveloped. Those in other Central American countries are well ahead of it," said James Vaughn, general manager of the U.S. textile company Rocedes S.A., which employs 1,150 Nicaraguans in its free trade zone making jeans, pants, uniforms and boxer shorts.
The maquiladora zone in neighbouring Honduras employs 60,000 workers, six times Nicaragua's total, he said.

Since the start-up of Nicaragua's maquiladora zone in 1992, exports have more than doubled every year, rising to $180 million in 1996 from $7 million in 1992, according Ministry of the Economy figures. Officials expect maquiladora exports to reach $212 million this year.
"If the government does the needed improvements in the facilities and labour code, there is no reason the maquiladora zone cannot continue doubling every year," Vaughn said.

Nicaragua's maquiladora zone offers the lowest rental costs in Central America -- factory space rents for an average of $2.50 per square meter -- and low labour costs, with a worker making about $100 a month, maquiladora zone President Gilberto Wong said.

But problems remain. Located on the outskirts of the capital Managua near the international airport, Nicaragua's maquiladora zone is landlocked, lacking a decent port in Nicaragua, which raises freight costs, Vaughn said.
"Our exports are transported by truck to ports in Honduras or Costa Rica, which costs us an extra $1,000 per container coming and going," Vaughn said.
